newsitem.title: USA: PLO leader arrives for White House talks.
newsitem.headline: PLO leader arrives for White House talks.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat arrived in Washington on Sunday, opening a four-day visit to the United States that includes talks with President Bill Clinton at the White House on Monday.

Arafat's plane landed at Andrews Air Force Base in nearby Maryland, a military spokesman said. The PLO leader planned to meet World Bank representatives and State Department officials on Sunday night.

In his discussions with Clinton, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and other U.S. officials, Arafat was expected to voice his concern over Israel's recent decision to build a new settlement for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem.

Israel captured Arab East Jerusalem along with the rest of the West Bank and Gaza Strip in the 1967 Middle East War. In a move not recognised by the international community, it annexed East Jerusalem, declaring it part of an indivisible capital.

The Palestinians want to establish an independent state in the occupied territories with East Jerusalem as capital. They saw the Israeli move as an attempt to cement Israel's hold over the entire city.

In an interview earlier on Sunday, Hanan Ashrawi, the Palestinian minister of higher education, said that Arafat would stress to Clinton the threat to the peace process posed by the Israeli government's action on new settlements.

"It's up to the U.S. to undertake its responsibility to demonstrate that it is not just evenhanded but it is committed to the peace process itself," she said. "It is imperative that the U.S. take a clear position on Jerusalem and settlements and not allow these violations."

Ashrawi said, "We take it for granted the U.S. policy and peace agreements clearly indicate that building of a new settlement in Jerusalem is not only illegal but is extremely destructive and an act of extreme provocation and incitement that could lead the whole peace process to unravel."
"It's very clear the Palestinian people are not going to sit back and accept the implication of the Israeli decison," she said, adding that their mood was "extremely volatile."
Arafat suggested on Saturday that he could declare a Palestinian state in response to the the approved construction of thousands of new Jewish homes in East Jerusalem.

"We are supposed to declare the setting up of a Palestinian state in five years but what would happen if I declare it right here? What would he (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu) do then? It's tit-for-tat and we have our weapons too," he told an emergency session of the Arab League in Cairo.
Netanyahu warned on Sunday that such a declaration would bring an end to peace moves.
"It will be a serious mistake, a severe mistake, that will bring a halt to the entire process," he told members of his Likud Party in Tel Aviv.

The United States criticised Israel's decision to build the new housing, saying it complicated an already complex situation and was not a step that would "build confidence and trust." The White House communicated its view to Netanyahu's government last week.
